messages: CPC has sent Tamhini three proposed adjustments on its AY 2026–27 return, ₹80,37,340 in all. Mahesh says all three should go. Tell me which we agree to, which we fight, and with what proof.
The return was due on 21 November 2026 after the CBDT extension; keep that date beside every payment. Draft reply on my desk by Friday the 22nd.

body: Hi Kunal,
The CPC notice came in tonight; attached. I think all three should go:
- Bonus is fully paid. Workmen on 21 October, staff on 27 November. The return date was extended to 21 November anyway.
- PF was paid, only a few weeks late, and every rupee reached the fund.

Attaching what I have. Tell me if you need anything else.

documents.title: Kunal’s draft · Grounds and statement of facts
documents.letterhead: Bapat Venkatesh & Co., Chartered Accountants · direct tax
documents.subject: Tamhini Drivetech · AY 2026–27 · first appeal against the intimation of 17 March 2027
body: ## Statement of facts
1. The return for AY 2026–27, due on 21-11-2026 under section 139(1) as extended by the CBDT, was filed on 27-10-2026. Bonus of ₹68,00,000 for FY 2025–26 was provided in the accounts.
2. ₹61,20,000 of it was paid to workmen on 21-10-2026 and ₹6,80,000 to staff on 27-11-2026.
3. In its response of 27-01-2027 the appellant agreed to ₹6,80,000 and disputed ₹61,20,000, with the bank statement and the bonus register.
4. The intimation of 17-03-2027 added the whole ₹68,00,000.
## Grounds of appeal
1. The CPC erred in adding ₹61,20,000 of bonus paid on 21-10-2026, before the due date for the return under section 139(1).
2. The CPC erred in disregarding the bank statement and the bonus register filed with the appellant’s response of 27-01-2027.
3. The appellant craves leave to add, alter or withdraw any ground.

annotations.text: Fine. File once Amol verifies – M.O.

body: Sir/Madam,

1. Bonus, ₹68,00,000. We disagree as to ₹61,20,000, paid to workmen on 21 October 2026, before the due date for the return under section 139(1); bank statement and bonus register enclosed. We agree to ₹6,80,000, paid to staff on 27 November 2026.

tasks.title: Read the notice

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand your notes on the notice to Kunal?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change these answers after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Kunal. These answers are now read-only.

tasks.prompt: Before any figure, read the notice the way Kunal will: what it is, why it quotes the 1961 Act, when the reply is due, and what follows if the CPC still disagrees. Varun has left the tracker’s respond-⁠by column blank for you.
hints: Look at the year the return is for, not the date on the notice.
The notice itself says how long Tamhini has, and from when.

options.text: A scrutiny notice: an officer will examine Tamhini’s books and records for the year
options.why: Scrutiny comes with its own notice and an officer’s questions. This one is processing: the CPC compared the return with the tax audit report.

options.text: A proposal: the CPC plans to add three audit-report items it says the return missed
options.why: Nothing is added yet. The CPC must consider Tamhini’s response before it makes any of these adjustments.

options.text: A demand: tax on ₹80,37,340 is payable within 30 days
options.why: No tax is payable yet. A demand comes only with the intimation, after the adjustments are made.

options.text: A penalty notice: Tamhini is charged with under-reporting its income for the year
options.why: Nothing here is a penalty. It is a proposal made on processing, and Tamhini can answer each item.

questions.text: Amol sir asks why a notice issued in 2027 still quotes the 1961 Act. What is the answer?

options.text: The CPC slipped: from 1 April 2026 every notice should quote the 2025 Act
options.why: No slip. The date of the notice doesn’t decide it; the year it is about does, and FY 2025–26 began before 1 April 2026.

options.text: The 2025 Act sets the procedure now; the 1961 Act only supplies the old rules
options.why: The 2025 Act’s transition rule covers procedure too: proceedings for earlier years are carried out as the 1961 Act provides.

options.text: FY 2025–26 began before 1 April 2026, so the 1961 Act governs it, appeals included
options.why: Proceedings for years that began before 1 April 2026 stay under the 1961 Act, notices and appeals included, even when they start later.

options.text: The notice follows the 1961 Act, but an appeal in 2027 goes under the 2025 Act
options.why: The same rule names appeals. An appeal for FY 2025–26 goes under the 1961 Act, in Form 35, whenever it is filed.

questions.text: What goes in the tracker’s respond-⁠by column?

options.text: Wednesday 10 February 2027: 30 days from the date of issue
options.why: The notice gives 30 days from its issue on 11 January. Diarise 10 February, and plan to file well before it.

options.text: Wednesday 31 March 2027: the day the financial year closes
options.why: The year-end has nothing to do with it. The clock started when the notice was issued, on 11 January.

options.text: 30 days from the day Tamhini first opens the notice on the portal
options.why: The clock runs from the date of issue printed on the notice, not from the day anyone reads it.

options.text: Leave it blank: the CPC waits for as long as Tamhini takes
options.why: It doesn’t wait. With no response in 30 days, it makes the adjustments.

questions.text: If the CPC still adds an item after reading the reply, what then?

options.text: A scrutiny assessment starts, and the point is argued before an officer there
options.why: Processing doesn’t turn into scrutiny on its own. The CPC sends an intimation, and that is what Tamhini takes further.

options.text: Tamhini keeps replying to the same notice until the CPC finally agrees with it
options.why: Once the CPC has decided, that notice is closed. The next step is against the intimation, not another reply.

options.text: The amount waits for next year’s return and is set right in that year
options.why: No. The intimation still follows, with the addition and a demand for AY 2026–27. An addition you dispute is fought in that year’s proceedings.

options.text: An intimation follows; Tamhini can appeal it in Form 35 within 30 days of service
options.why: The intimation is appealable. Form 35 goes in within 30 days of the day it was served; a late appeal needs a reason the appellate authority accepts.

tasks.title: Agree or disagree, item by item

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand your three calls to Kunal?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change them after this. Kunal reads them before the reply is drafted.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Kunal. These calls are now read-only.

tasks.prompt: Take each proposed adjustment to its papers. Decide whether Tamhini agrees, agrees in part or disagrees; say what decides it; give the amount in dispute; and pick the papers that prove it. Kunal reads your calls before the reply is drafted.
hints: For PF, check which year’s rule applies before you lean on the return date.
Before you agree to anything, check whether the computation already added it back.

options.label: Whether it was paid by the return due date
Whether the return already added it back
Whether it reached the fund by the PF law’s date
Whether it was provided in the books
Computation of income for the return
PF register for Oct 2025 to Jan 2026

items.label: Bonus
items.prompt: Proposed ₹68,00,000: shown as not paid on 25 September 2026, the date of the tax audit report.
items.note: Bonus: the workmen’s ₹61,20,000 left the bank on 21 October, before the 21 November due date; the staff ₹6,80,000 went on 27 November, after it. Dispute ₹61,20,000 with the bank page and register; agree the rest. The ledger shows only the provision.

items.label: Employees’ PF
items.prompt: Proposed ₹2,77,340: the employees’ share for November 2025.
items.note: PF: November 2025’s employees’ share reached the fund on 27 January 2026. For FY 2025–26 the test is the PF law’s date, and the return date doesn’t help. Agree. Fighting it would cost us credibility on the bonus.

items.label: Leave encashment
items.prompt: Proposed ₹9,60,000: the year’s provision, not paid.
items.note: Leave encashment: line 5 of Tamhini’s computation already adds back ₹9,60,000, under other disallowances, so the CPC missed it. Agreeing would tax it twice. Dispute all of it and enclose the computation.

tasks.title: Draft the reply

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand the draft reply to Kunal?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change it after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Kunal. The draft is now read-only.

tasks.prompt: Build Tamhini’s reply to the CPC from the lines below, one point to a paragraph; Milind reads it before it is filed. Pick the best line for each part: every amount and date must match the papers.
hints: Each paragraph says agree or disagree, the amount, and the paper that proves it.

options.text: Sub: Assessment year 2026–27, PAN ZHDCT5940H. Our response to the adjustments proposed under section 143(1)(a) of the Income-⁠tax Act, 1961, in your notice issued on 11 January 2027 (DIN CPC/2627/G22/1716455031).
options.why: Year, PAN, section and DIN: the CPC can match the reply to its notice without a phone call.

options.text: Sub: Tax year 2026–27, PAN ZHDCT5940H. Our response to the adjustments proposed under section 270(2) of the Income-⁠tax Act, 2025, in your notice issued on 11 January 2027 (DIN CPC/2627/G22/1716455031).
options.why: FY 2025–26 is assessment year 2026–27, a 1961-⁠Act year. Section 270(2) is the new Act’s version, for tax year 2026–27 onwards.

options.text: Sub: Assessment year 2026–27, PAN ZHDCT5940H. Our appeal against the demand raised under section 143(1) of the Income-⁠tax Act, 1961, in your notice issued on 11 January 2027 (DIN CPC/2627/G22/1716455031).
options.why: There is no demand yet and nothing to appeal. This is a response to a proposal.

options.text: 1. Bonus, ₹68,00,000. We disagree with all of it: ₹61,20,000 was paid to workmen on 21 October 2026 and ₹6,80,000 to staff on 27 November 2026, both before the CPC processed the return; the bank statement and the bonus register are enclosed.
options.why: The test is the due date for the return, 21 November 2026, not the date of processing. The staff part missed it, so the whole bonus can’t be disputed.

options.text: 1. Bonus, ₹68,00,000. We disagree with all of it: the full bonus was provided in the accounts for FY 2025–26, the year in which it was earned, as the tax audit report itself shows; the bonus payable ledger is enclosed.
options.why: A provision is exactly what section 43B holds back until payment, and the ledger shows only the provision.

options.text: 1. Bonus, ₹68,00,000. We disagree as to ₹61,20,000, paid to workmen on 21 October 2026, before the due date for the return under section 139(1); bank statement and bonus register enclosed. We agree to ₹6,80,000, paid to staff on 27 November 2026.
options.why: Each part on its own date, with the papers that prove the part disputed. Conceding ₹6,80,000 gives the rest its weight.

options.text: 2. Employees’ PF, ₹2,77,340. We disagree: the November 2025 contribution was credited on 27 January 2026, well before the due date for the return under section 139(1).
options.why: That is the rule from tax year 2026–27. For FY 2025–26 the date is the PF law’s, and section 43B does not help with employees’ contributions.

options.text: 2. Employees’ PF, ₹2,77,340. We agree: the November 2025 contribution was credited on 27 January 2026, after the due date under the provident fund law.
options.why: Short and true. For that year the law closes it.

options.text: 2. Employees’ PF, ₹2,77,340. We disagree: the full November 2025 contribution reached the employees’ accounts, only some weeks late, so nothing was withheld.
options.why: Paid late but in full still fails that year’s test: credit by the PF law’s date. The delay is the whole point.

options.text: 3. Leave encashment, ₹9,60,000. We disagree: the return as filed already adds it back, under other disallowances, as our computation of income (copy enclosed) shows. Adding it again would tax it twice.
options.why: The answer sits in Tamhini’s own computation, line 5. Point to it and the CPC can see the double count.

options.text: 3. Leave encashment, ₹9,60,000. We agree: it was provided for FY 2025–26 and was not paid by the due date for the return, so section 43B holds it back for that year.
options.why: True of the law, wrong for this return: the computation already adds it back. Agreeing would tax it twice.

options.text: 3. Leave encashment, ₹9,60,000. We disagree: leave encashment is part of the salary cost, which section 43B does not cover, so the provision is allowed.
options.why: Section 43B covers it: clause (f) is any sum an employer owes in lieu of leave at the employee’s credit. The computation answers this one.

options.text: We request that all three adjustments, ₹80,37,340 in all, be dropped and that the return be accepted as filed. The papers named above are enclosed.
options.why: That contradicts the three points above, which agree ₹9,57,340. The request is the line the CPC acts on, so it must add up to what we argued.

options.text: We request that the adjustments be limited to ₹9,57,340 (bonus ₹6,80,000 and PF ₹2,77,340) and that ₹70,80,000 be dropped. The papers named above are enclosed.
options.why: The ask adds up to the three points: ₹9,57,340 agreed, ₹70,80,000 disputed, ₹80,37,340 in all.

options.text: We request that the adjustments be limited to ₹2,77,340 (PF) and that ₹77,60,000 be dropped. The papers named above are enclosed.
options.why: That disputes the staff bonus too. ₹6,80,000 was paid after the due date, so the right limit is ₹9,57,340.

tasks.title: Index the appeal set
tasks.prompt: Tuesday 23 March 2027. The CPC’s intimation of 17 March dropped leave encashment but added the whole ₹68,00,000 of bonus. Milind will appeal ₹61,20,000 of it in Form 35, within 30 days of service. Varun has pulled ten papers from the file. Mark each one: does it go in the appeal set?
hints: Only what is still in dispute goes in, with the papers Form 35 asks for.
The appeal needs the order appealed against, the fee and proof that the tax on the returned income is paid.

items.label: Kunal’s draft grounds and statement of facts
items.note: The core of the set. Ground 1 names ₹61,20,000 and the day it was paid; the statement of facts tells the story in dates. Form 35 asks for both.

items.label: Varun’s first draft of the grounds
items.note: It appeals all ₹68,00,000, including the ₹6,80,000 we agreed to in our own reply. That contradicts us on paper. Out.

items.label: Intimation under section 143(1), 17 March 2027
items.note: The order appealed against, with its DIN. It was served by e-mail on 17 March, and the 30 days run from that date.

items.label: Appeal fee challan
items.note: Total income as computed is over ₹2 lakh, so the fee is ₹1,000. Form 35 asks for the challan’s details.

items.label: Advance-tax challans and TDS credit
items.note: An appeal is admitted only if the tax on the returned income is paid. These challans and the TDS credit show it was: ₹1,94,00,000.

items.label: The CPC’s notice, our reply and its acknowledgement
items.note: Ground 2 says the CPC disregarded our response, so the notice, the response and its acknowledgement go in. They show we disputed ₹61,20,000, with proof, before the CPC decided.

items.label: October bank page and bonus register
items.note: The proof itself. It went in with our reply in January, so it is already on record.

items.label: Computation, line 5: leave encashment added back
items.note: This page was our proof on leave encashment, and the CPC accepted it. Nothing is left to argue there, so it stays in the file.

items.label: PF register, Oct 2025 to Jan 2026
items.note: We agreed to PF in January, and the CPC added just that ₹2,77,340. Not in dispute, not in the set.

items.label: Mahesh’s mail of 11 January
items.note: A client’s mail is not evidence, and this one is wrong about the staff part. The bank page already proves the date.

wrap.text: ₹9,57,340 agreed and ₹70,80,000 disputed, each point on its own paper, so the appeal has only ₹61,20,000 left to argue. Amol verifies Form 35 on 9 April, a week inside the 30 days.

wrapPartial.text: Not all of this would get past Milind yet. Read each note against the paper it names, and keep asking what is still in dispute.

wrapRetry.text: Begin with the year the notice is about, then put each item beside its own paper: the bank dates for the bonus, the PF register for PF, Tamhini’s computation for leave encashment. Try again with those three open.

passNeeds.note: The three calls decide the pass: get more of them right, with the amount and the proof.
The reply needs more of its lines right before this passes.

model.intro: Agree ₹9,57,340, dispute ₹70,80,000. The bonus splits on its payment dates; PF is closed by that year’s law; leave encashment is already added back in the return. When the CPC still adds the workmen’s bonus, the appeal set carries only that point and its proof.

rows.r: Dispute ₹61,20,000, paid 21 October 2026; agree ₹6,80,000, paid 27 November 2026
Agree: credited on 27 January 2026, after the PF law’s date
Dispute all: the return already adds it back
rows.e: Computation of income for the return, line 5

items: Form 35, with the statement of facts and the grounds (Kunal’s draft)
The intimation of 17 March 2027, with its DIN; served that day by e-mail
The challans and TDS credit for the tax on the returned income, ₹1,94,00,000
The CPC’s notice, our reply and its acknowledgement
The October bank page and the bonus register, filed with the reply in January

blocks.text: Left in the file: Varun’s draft, the computation, the PF register and Mahesh’s mail.

Under the 2025 Act, for tax year 2026–27 onwards, the same proposal comes under section 270(2), still with 30 days to respond; a first appeal goes in Form 99 within 30 days of service; and employees’ PF counts if credited by the return due date.
Agreeing to PF and the staff bonus is what makes the rest believable. A reply that fights every item reads like a template.

principles: Name the year first: FY 2025–26 is still a 1961-⁠Act year, even in 2027.
Take each item to its own paper: agree what the law closes, dispute what the evidence wins.
File the proof with the reply, so it is already on record if the matter goes to appeal.

interview.q: A notice comes in for a client. What do you do first?
interview.checking: Whether you read a notice in order and answer it point by point, with proof.
outline: Read the year, the section, what it proposes and the reply date; tell my senior the same day.
Take each item to its papers: return, audit report, books; agree what the law closes, prove the rest.
In the simulation I answered {adj} proposed adjustments that way[[, disputing {disp} with evidence]].

interview.q: Which Act governs a notice for FY 2025–26, and why does it matter?
interview.checking: Whether you can place an earlier year under the right Act during the change-over.
outline: The 1961 Act governs proceedings for years that began before 1 April 2026, even notices issued later.
In the simulation it settled the PF item: that year’s law allowed no relief for a late credit.
From tax year 2026–27 the same proposal is section 270(2), and the PF test is the return date.
